title: Semantic differential analysis of the soundscape in urban open public spaces
research_question: To identify factors that characterise the soundscape in urban open public spaces, to understand how people evaluate perceived soundscape, and to examine differences between designers and the general public in soundscape evaluation.

participants.description: Stage 1: 48 university students (18-25 years old, 30 males, 18 females, audiologically normal) in Sheffield, UK. Stage 2: 491 general public (users, not passers-by, over 40% below 24 years old, generally high education, many students/working people, more males than females) in Sheffield, UK. Stage 3: 223 architectural students in Sheffield, UK.
participants.recruitment: Stage 1: University students. Stage 2: Randomly selected users in public squares. Stage 3: Architectural students.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four typical urban open public spaces in Sheffield, UK: Union Square (near roundabout, heavy traffic, loud music, birds, pedestrian/bike, conversations), Devonshire Green (large green space, skate park, distant traffic, birds, pedestrian/bike, construction noise), Barkers Pool (city centre, pedestrian area, light traffic, conversations, footsteps, skateboarding, wind, street singers, music from surrounding buildings), and Peace Gardens (city centre, multi-story buildings, busy road, water fountains/cascades, distant traffic, chatting, children's shouting, demolition noise in autumn/winter).

measures.instrument: 7-point bipolar rating scale (28 indices, reduced to 18 for main study)
5-point scale (1: very quiet to 5: very noisy)
5-point scale (1: very comfortable to 5: very uncomfortable)
Classification as favourite, neither favourite nor annoying, or annoying
Questionnaire items for gender, age, education, occupation
One-minute Leq, Leq,90, Leq,50, Leq,10 (dBA) measurements
Selection from a given list (architectural students)

findings.quote: the scores for acoustic comfort are significantly lower than those for sound level (p < 0.05)
strong positive linear correlation between the measured sound level Leq and the subjective evaluation of sound level (p < 0.01)
the correlation between the Leq and the acoustic comfort evaluation is non-linear and R2 is also much lower, at only 0.404 in the Barkers Pool and 0.541 in the Peace Gardens.

findings.antecedent: Presence of pleasant sounds (music or water)
findings.quote: introducing a pleasant sound like music or water can considerably improve the acoustic comfort, even when its sound level is rather high.

findings.consequent: Preference for sounds relating to nature, culture, or human activities
findings.quote: With the increase of age, people were generally more favourable to sounds relating to nature, culture or human activities.
Table 4 the evaluation of bird songs is compared between different age groups.

findings.consequent: Favourability/tolerance of street music and mechanical sounds
findings.quote: young people were more favourable to or tolerant of sounds like street music and mechanical sounds.
Between males and females the difference in sound preference was not statistically significant.
with the increase of education level people tend to prefer natural sounds more
but are more annoyed by mechanical sounds.
Compared to education level, the influence of occupation (e.g. students, working people, others) on the sound preference is less significant

findings.consequent: Semantic factor 'relaxation' (comfort-discomfort, quiet-noisy, pleasant-unpleasant, natural-artificial, like-dislike, gentle-harsh)
findings.quote: factor 1 (26%) is mainly associated with relaxation, including comfort-discomfort, quiet-noisy, pleasant-unpleasant, natural-artificial, like-dislike and gentle-harsh.
Factor 2 (12%) is generally associated with communication, including social-unsocial, meaningful-meaningless, calming-agitating, and smooth-rough.
Factor 3 (8%) is mostly associated with spatiality, including varied-simple, echoed-deadly and far-close.
Factor 4 (7%) is principally related to dynamics, including hard-soft and fast-slow.

findings.antecedent: Presence of a special/dominant sound source (e.g., high level demolition noise)
findings.quote: when there is a special/dominant sound source, the results of factor analysis could be considerably affected.

findings.antecedent: Participant group (architectural students vs. general public)
findings.consequent: Number of factors identified in semantic differential analysis
findings.quote: with the architectural students there are slightly more factors

findings.antecedent: Participant group (architectural students vs. general public)
findings.quote: the evaluation of the architectural students is more diverse than that of the general public

findings.antecedent: Urban open public spaces with natural sounds and considerable green spaces (Peace Gardens, Devonshire Green)
findings.consequent: Evaluation scores for comfort-discomfort, pleasant-unpleasant, quiet-noisy (architectural students)
findings.quote: in the two squares with natural sounds and considerable green spaces, namely the Peace Gardens and Devonshire Green, the scores for the first three indices are systematically higher than those in the other two squares

findings.consequent: Evaluation scores for comfort-discomfort, pleasant-unpleasant, quiet-noisy, social-unsocial (architectural students vs. general public)
findings.quote: for the Peace Gardens the scores of the architectural students are significantly higher, according to a series of Independent Samples T-tests (p<0.05), for all four indices

findings.consequent: Evaluation scores (architectural students vs. general public)
findings.quote: For the Barkers Pool, the difference between architectural students and the general public is much less, and generally there is no statistically significant difference.

findings.antecedent: Environmental factors (sound, view, temperature, air quality, sun, security, humidity, wind)
findings.consequent: Perceived importance of sound as an environmental factor (architectural students)
findings.quote: sound is a rather significant consideration, ranked as second/third on the list.

findings.consequent: Perceived importance for choosing a location to sit/relax (architectural students)
findings.quote: when you choose a location to sit/relax in this square, is the acoustic environment an important factor? The percentage of answering 'yes' is 63%, 87%, 54% and 75% in the Union Square, Devonshire Green, Barkers Pool, and Peace Gardens, respectively.

mechanisms: People's tolerance to noise, where they may find a noisy environment acoustically comfortable due to other factors.
The type of sound source (e.g., pleasant music/water vs. unpleasant construction noise) influences acoustic comfort and overall soundscape evaluation.
Users choose locations within a space according to their preferences and activities, influencing their satisfaction with the acoustic environment.
Foreground sounds (e.g., fountains, demolition work) can contribute to specific semantic factors in soundscape evaluation.
Expertise and cultural priors influence the perception and evaluation of soundscapes, leading to differences between designers and the general public.
moderators: Specific site (Barkers Pool vs. Peace Gardens)
Participant group (architectural students vs. general public)
implementation_implications: Designers should consider the sound environment as an important factor in urban open public spaces.
Urban soundscape design should account for different preferences based on demographic factors like age and education.
Introducing pleasant sounds (e.g., music, water features) can significantly improve acoustic comfort, even in environments with relatively high sound levels.
Different evaluation and weighting systems for soundscape design may be needed for different types of urban squares.
Special attention should be paid to the characteristics and potential unpleasantness of dominant sound sources in urban spaces.

Average evaluation score of typical indices in the four squares, by the architectural student group (stage three) and by the general public (stage two).

limitations: Some semantic differential indices were seldom selected/evaluated or not well-understood by interviewees in the second stage of survey.

The factor analysis covered only 53% of the total variance, which is lower than typical product sound quality studies, possibly due to the significant variations in urban open public spaces and sound source characteristics.
The demographic profiles of the architectural students and the general public were different, which might influence the direct comparison of their evaluations.

environmental_features: visual characteristics of urban spaces (e.g., presence of greenery, buildings, open space)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Participants spent approximately 10-15 minutes at each evaluation site.
control_conditions: Comparison across multiple distinct urban open public spaces (e.g., urban squares, parks, busy streets) with varying acoustic and visual characteristics.

instruments_used.name: Soundscape Semantic Differential Questionnaire
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire employing bipolar adjective scales (e.g., pleasant-unpleasant, calm-chaotic, vibrant-monotonous, quiet-loud) to assess subjective perception of the soundscape attributes.

instruments_used.name: Sound Level Meter
instruments_used.description: Used to measure A-weighted equivalent continuous sound pressure levels (LAeq) and other acoustic parameters (e.g., L10, L90) at the study sites.

stimulus_images.description: Photographs of the urban open public spaces where soundscape evaluations were conducted, showing the visual context of the acoustic stimuli.
